title: A Inventory for the Postcards
premise: Rafael Okafor has spent eleven years writing postcards to his mother's address — a house that burned the night his sister Adaeze disappeared, an event the family buried under a new surname and a perfected public smile. When a stranger named Nour appears at his father's funeral speaking the old family name, she reveals she was the child who saw what happened that night and has been receiving Rafael's postcards at a forwarding address no one should know. As the city schedules the burned lot for demolition, Rafael and Nour must excavate the truth together: that Adaeze survived, that their father chose silence to protect the family's standing, and that the postcards were never going to a dead woman but to a living sister who never answered. The novel ends on demolition day, when Adaeze finally arrives at the lot, and Rafael must choose between the loyalty of inherited silence and the truth that might finally let them all survive it.
about_author: Astrid Oyelaran is a former archivist for a municipal records office who spent years cataloguing condemned properties and the mail that kept arriving for them. She writes from Lagos and Lisbon about families that survive by forgetting.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. At his father's wake, Rafael performs grief flawlessly, deflecting condolences with the practiced smile he learned as a boy. We learn he writes weekly postcards to a burned house. Emotional beat: the loneliness of being fluent in a language of concealment.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A stranger at the graveside says 'Okonkwo' — the family name erased after the fire — and watches him too closely. He confronts her; she hands him one of his own postcards, postmarked last month. Beat: the floor drops out of his controlled world.

chapters.title: Nour
chapters.summary: Nour's POV. She explains she received his postcards through a forwarding arrangement made by her late aunt, who once worked for the Okonkwo household. She knows something about the night of the fire. Beat: wary alliance between two keepers of other people's secrets.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. He sorts his mother's belongings and finds a locked tin labeled in Adaeze's handwriting. His uncle warns him to let the past stay past. Beat: inheritance revealed as a burden, not a gift.

chapters.title: The Lot on Ilupeju Street
chapters.summary: Nour's POV. They visit the burned house together; Rafael hasn't returned in eleven years. A demolition notice is stapled to the fence — thirty days. Beat: dread mixed with a strange relief that time is running out.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Kept
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. An elderly neighbor remembers the fire differently than the official record: two children left the house that night, not one. Beat: the first crack in the story Rafael built his life on.

chapters.title: The Tin Opens
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Inside the tin: photographs, a hospital bracelet, and letters from Adaeze written after the fire — addressed to their mother, all unopened. Beat: grief curdling into anger at his parents' lie.

chapters.title: Loyalty Is a Kind of Silence
chapters.summary: Nour's POV. Nour confesses her aunt helped smuggle the injured Adaeze away and swore her to secrecy until death. Rafael accuses her of complicity. Beat: the alliance fractures under the weight of loyalty vs. truth.

chapters.title: Postcards, Returned
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. He visits the postal depot and learns every postcard he sent was collected by the same hand for years — someone was reading them. Beat: humiliation and hope tangled together; he was writing to someone alive.

chapters.title: The Uncle's Version
chapters.summary: Uncle Emeka's testimony via Rafael's POV. The father's version: Adaeze started the fire, fled shame, and the name change protected the surviving son. Beat: a plausible story that fits too neatly, and Rafael wanting desperately to believe it.

chapters.title: Hospital Records
chapters.summary: Nour's POV. Nour pulls strings at a clinic where her aunt volunteered and finds a burn victim admitted that night under a false name — discharged to a convent upcountry. Beat: a thread pulled taut; the truth has an address.

chapters.title: The Convent Road
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. They travel together, bickering, circling their private wounds. At the convent they learn Sister Ada left three years ago, leaving only a forwarding request — to the burned house. Beat: she was coming home, always.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Among his mother's effects he finds drafts of replies to Adaeze, never mailed, each one more afraid than the last. Beat: understanding his mother's paralysis; the price of survival was paid by everyone.

chapters.title: Demolition Date Moved Up
chapters.summary: Nour's POV. A developer accelerates the demolition to ten days. Nour realizes her aunt's old landlord connection may be why the postcards kept flowing — and why someone wants the lot cleared now. Beat: external pressure compresses the clock.

chapters.title: The Developer's Interest
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The developer turns out to be connected to Uncle Emeka's business dealings; clearing the lot buries evidence of what really happened. Beat: the conspiracy is banal, financial, and utterly human.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Wake House
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Rafael publicly demands the truth from Emeka before the extended family. Emeka admits the father paid for silence after learning Adaeze lived — protecting the family name over the daughter. Beat: climax of the loyalty-vs-truth theme; the family shatters.

chapters.title: What Rafael Saw
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, flashback woven into present. Memory returns: he was there that night; he saw Adaeze pull their mother from the fire and run rather than face blame. He has always known. Beat: devastating self-reckoning — he is not innocent of the silence.

chapters.title: The Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Nour's POV. Nour writes a postcard of her own and mails it to the convent forwarding address, betting love travels faster than demolition. Rafael, furious then broken, adds a line: 'Come home before they take the walls down.' Beat: surrender to hope.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Waiting. He stops performing the smile; conversations lengthen; he tells a neighbor the truth just to practice saying it aloud. Beat: quiet transformation — survival redefined as honesty rather than endurance.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: Both POVs. No word from Adaeze. Rafael stands guard at the lot overnight, prepared to chain himself to the fence. Nour brings food and stays. Beat: stillness before the storm; two strangers now kin in purpose.

chapters.title: The Woman at the Fence
chapters.summary: Climax, Rafael's POV. As machines arrive, a woman in a nun's habit walks through the crowd. Adaeze. She holds every postcard he ever sent, rubber-banded, read soft with handling. She says the name nobody uses, and gives it back to him. Beat: catharsis; the truth spoken at last, publicly, on the ruined ground.

chapters.title: An Inventory for the Postcards
chapters.summary: Resolution, both POVs. Months later: the lot becomes a small memorial garden; the family name restored on a plaque. Rafael writes one final postcard — to himself, at his own address — listing what survived: a sister, a friend, a true story. Beat: peace earned, not given; inheritance rewritten.
